data.name: Tom vs. The Armies of Hell
data.detailed_description:
Tom vs. the Armies of Hell is a challenging indie Action-Adventure game from Darkmire Entertainment. You play Tom, a down-trodden software-engineer turned reluctant half-demon hero when an experiment gone awry sends his entire office complex plummeting into Hell.

Armed with an experimental gun that turns captured souls into high-tech, multi-colored death, as well as his newly acquired demonic powers, Tom must not only survive, but also unravel the mystery of what caused this "accident", and how he can get home. Along the way Tom will be aided (or more accurately, bossed around) by Beezle, the purple imp that saved him from the initial demonic invasion. Together they'll face a horde of mindless ghouls, vicious demons, and an army of magically animated junk automatons, just for starters.

So grab your trusty Soul Blaster x9000, duct-tape some phone-books to your extremities, and blast your way through the plains of eternal damnation!

Key Features

  • Enjoy a story-driven single-player campaign -- just like mom used to make!
  • Blast away with a dynamic gun system, where absorbed souls turn into rainbow-colored death.
  • Laugh out loud with an original, humorous story revealed across six challenging levels.
  • Stare at beautifully animated 2D and in-game cutscenes.
  • Mow through hordes of procedurally placed enemies. No two playthroughs are exactly alike!

data.short_description: Meet Tom -- a software engineer turned reluctant half-demon hero who must fight his way out of Hell by turning souls into demon-searing weapons. Blast your way back to your 9-to-5 in this hilarious, isometric indie action-adventure game.

reviews.review:
This game has a very nice graphical style and a great sense of humor. The gameplay is fun except for one glaringly obvious problem that hurts the game dearly. The simple fact is that most players will not want to try the "normal" or "hard" modes when the first mode is already annoying and ridiculous (particularly with the boss battles). The game also makes another classic design mistake. Take the boss battle in level 2, it's actually a pair of back to back battles with no chance to heal or anything in between. Being poorly designed, its also setup so that if you die in the second battle, you have to redo the first one again...

NOTE: There is a patch in the works addressing this difficulty issue, and so I will need to re-evaluate this review when that comes out as it wouldn't be fair to the developer if I don't.

Tom vs. The Armies of Hell simply fails to understand that its easiest mode is the gateway for new players to join. It fails here by being one of those games to follow the painfully misguided "difficulty for the sake of difficulty" design style, which has ruined countless games. The difficulty levels in this game are all shifted up by at least one, especially when it comes to the boss battles. The boss battles in the easiest game mode feel like what most games would call "hard mode", which is not intelligent design... Tom vs. The Armies of Hell is just another game that couldn't figure out the basic game design fact, that turning away new players makes it very hard to build a fanbase. Worse, it curses the game to a niche existence where it is doomed to decay forever in the void of obscurity. So this design style that already makes no sense in a game design context, makes even less sense in a business context...

Video games first and foremost are about entertainment and fun, not unnecessary effort retrying poorly designed levels 400 times (like this game's boss fights) or pointlessly trying to prove something by seeing how hard of nonsense you can beat. Beating such nonsense is irrelvant in the grand scheme of things, and therefore completely pointless (not to mention a collosal waste of time). Difficulty in video games is a double-edged sword. It can make a game much better if done well, or turn players away in droves when done poorly (as in this game). 

All too often, video game challenges are poorly designed (the boss fights in this game are no exception). You've no doubt seen them, the types of challenges that serve as a brick wall to artificially slow the player's progress by making the player bang his/her head on a proverbial brick wall for no good reason. Besides that, most challenges in video games (and this one) are lazy stuff thrown together in under 5 minutes through the use of one or more of three basic things: unreasonable time limits, unreasonable scoring goals, or unreasonable amounts of enemies or other hazards. Cheap BS like this is far too common in video games, and Tom vs. The Armies of Hell makes the same tired old mistakes (by putting very little thought into how its difficulty is designed).

It's unfortunate that so many developers put very little thought into game design or even bother to research it at all, as I have indeed done. It is a very important topic to know about if you're going to make games, which seems extremely obvious, and yet we still have a world with far too many examples of poor game design... And there is yet another basic rule of game design that this game breaks: the rule that when the player fails, they should feel that the failure was because they screwed up and not because the game is being cheap and unfair. Tom vs. The Armies of Hell heavily fails on this one.
